turns.label: A1
turns.question: Teach me cache scaling.
turns.answer:
Think about what happens when your computer's memory gets slammed during a heavy workload. If you only have one type of memory, it either gets too expensive to make huge or too slow to keep up. **Cache scaling** solves this bottleneck by combining different speeds of memory into a tiered system, handling peak demands without needing all expensive RAM [1].

In the lecture, this falls under intra and inter array data movement techniques [1]. Cache scaling specifically uses dynamic RAM as tier zero and an SSD as tier one [1]. This setup creates a large capacity secondary cache that sits between the DRAM and the SSD, keeping performance high when workloads peak [1]. 

Imagine a bustling restaurant kitchen. The chef keeps the ingredients they need this exact second on the cutting board right in front of them—that is your ultra-fast dynamic RAM (tier zero). The ingredients they need for the next hour stay in the walk-in fridge just steps away—that is your SSD (tier one). Instead of running all the way to the main off-site warehouse for every single item, the kitchen scales its capacity locally by tiering between the counter and the fridge, keeping service smooth even during the Friday night rush.

To test yourself: What are the specific roles of tier zero and tier one in cache scaling [1]?

Let's drop the restaurant analogy entirely and look at it through a shipping warehouse. 

In cache scaling, you are dealing with two specific layers working together [1]. 

**Tier zero** is dynamic RAM [1]. Think of this as the packing desk right by the loading dock—it holds only what the workers are packing this exact second, moving at top speed. 

**Tier one** is an SSD [1]. Think of this as the main shelving racks just behind the packing desk holding the broader inventory for the day. 

By tiering between that dynamic RAM and the SSD, the system creates a large-capacity secondary cache that keeps performance high when heavy workloads hit [1].

turns.label: B1
turns.question: Explain Transformation.
turns.answer:
A transformation matrix represents the mathematical relationship between two consecutive joints in a robotic arm, mapped from the previous joint to the current one [2]. To find this relationship, you multiply the individual **joint parameters** (which describe the relative position and orientation between connected axes) and **link parameters** (which describe the physical dimensions of the connecting member) [2]. 

To build intuition, imagine two hinged segments of a robotic arm where each segment has its own local coordinate system; the transformation matrix acts as the bridge that translates coordinates from the base of one segment into the coordinate system of the next. In the lecture's procedure, you derive this by first defining your parameters, building the individual matrices for the joint and link parameters, and then multiplying those matrices together to achieve the final complementation required to derive the overall arm matrix [3].

retries.label: A3-retry
retries.answer:
Take an enterprise database running a heavy transaction workload, like an online banking system processing thousands of customer account updates every second. 

**Tier zero** is dynamic RAM handling the active transactions right now [3]. When a customer clicks transfer, that record sits immediately in the dynamic RAM tier for ultra-fast reading and writing.

**Tier one** is an SSD holding the broader set of records needed across the day [3]. 

When a sudden surge of traffic hits—such as a morning rush of payroll deposits—the system uses cache tiering between that dynamic RAM and the SSD [3]. Instead of crashing or slowing down when the dynamic RAM fills up, the large-capacity secondary cache kicks in to absorb the peak workload without forcing every request down to the slower storage layer [3].
